title: One Index Over Both Filter Columns
description: Filtering on two columns with no matching index scans; a single composite index over both lets the engine seek straight to the rows.
narrative:
## Scenario
An inventory check looks up one product in one warehouse: `WHERE WarehouseId = 35 AND ProductId = 1235`. With no matching index, finding a handful of rows scans all 300,000.

## Why it's slow
There's no index on these columns, so it's a **Clustered Index Scan**. Neither column alone is very selective (50 warehouses, 6,000 products), but *together* they pin down just a few rows — so the ideal index covers **both**.

## What to look for
- A full scan for a query that targets one warehouse/product pair.
- Reads across the whole table to return a tiny result.

## The concept
When a query filters on several columns with `AND`, a single **composite index** over those columns lets SQL Server seek straight to the matching rows: `(WarehouseId, ProductId)`. It's far better than two separate single-column indexes (which the engine would have to combine) and far better than no index at all. INCLUDE `Qty` so the index also covers what you select.
hints: No index covers WarehouseId and ProductId together, so the whole table is scanned.
The two columns together are highly selective; one composite index over both lets the engine seek.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Inventory_Wh_Prod ON Inventory(WarehouseId, ProductId) INCLUDE (Qty);
